dialogue: Lost Wages, 1987. Eighty bucks. One polyester suit. Absolutely no reason to be this confident. Welcome to your big night, Larry.
Pink neon, palm trees, and a city that charges extra for sincerity. A free newspaper and a flower cart offer a promising start.
You pay $10 for flowers. Remaining funds: $60.
The regular lifts the whiskey in a toast and hands you the remote. 'Channel six. Bowling. The pins fall for me, at least.'
You select channel six. The bouncer gasps at a seven-ten split. Provide the password and the backstage door is yours.
Bouncer: 'Password first. And if anyone finds the remote, the finals are on channel six.'

Lefty polishes the same glass history forgot. The regular raises the whiskey you brought him. Championship bowling fills the television; the bouncer follows every frame. The bouncer controls the backstage door.
'Bellybutton,' you say with improbable confidence. The password checks out. The bowling has his attention; head backstage.
Between two questionable poems: 'BACKSTAGE PASSWORD: BELLYBUTTON.' You commit it to your least crowded brain cell.
Avocado tile, optimistic plumbing, and unusually useful graffiti. A dish beside the basin offers a free costume ring.
Taken: Costume ring. Your pockets ignore the laws of tailoring.
The cabaret is between shows. Promotional chocolates wait on a table, outnumbered by feathers. The fire escape has lost a step; a rope tied to the railing could bridge the gap.
Taken: Candy. Your pockets ignore the laws of tailoring.
Chrome, carpet, and the sound of wallets clearing their throats. A disco pass rests in a clean ashtray. The cashier offers comeback cash if your luck gets too personal.
Taken: Disco pass. Your pockets ignore the laws of tailoring.
Didi takes your hand. 'Show me what those trousers can do.' Your signature move resembles a printer jam. She laughs and pulls you into the beat.
Didi takes the candy with a smile. 'Perfect for the show. Keep this up and I'll put your name in lights. Small lights. Don't get cocky.'
Didi takes the costume ring with a smile. 'Perfect for the show. Keep this up and I'll put your name in lights. Small lights. Don't get cocky.'
The bass line has a mortgage. Didi, a stage designer off the clock and on the beat, catches your eye. A wall phone connects to the stage crew. A tied coil of spare rope hangs beside the DJ booth.
Didi accepts the final prop with a grin. Didi: 'Sweet, funny, and wonderfully overdressed. Call my stage manager at 555-0987 about that spare rope. Tell him you're with me. He'll be jealous.'

dialogue: Lost Wages, 1987. Eighty bucks. One polyester suit. Absolutely no reason to be this confident. Welcome to your big night, Larry.
Pink neon, palm trees, and a city that charges extra for sincerity. A free newspaper and a flower cart offer a promising start.
You pay $10 for flowers. Remaining funds: $60.
The regular lifts the whiskey in a toast and hands you the remote. 'Channel six. Bowling. The pins fall for me, at least.'
You select channel six. The bouncer gasps at a seven-ten split. Provide the password and the backstage door is yours.
Bouncer: 'Password first. And if anyone finds the remote, the finals are on channel six.'

Lefty polishes the same glass history forgot. The regular raises the whiskey you brought him. Championship bowling fills the television; the bouncer follows every frame. The bouncer controls the backstage door.
'Bellybutton,' you say with improbable confidence. The password checks out. The bowling has his attention; head backstage.
Between two questionable poems: 'BACKSTAGE PASSWORD: BELLYBUTTON.' You commit it to your least crowded brain cell.
Avocado tile, optimistic plumbing, and unusually useful graffiti. A dish beside the basin offers a free costume ring.
Taken: Costume ring. Your pockets ignore the laws of tailoring.
The cabaret is between shows. Promotional chocolates wait on a table, outnumbered by feathers. The fire escape has lost a step; a rope tied to the railing could bridge the gap.
Taken: Candy. Your pockets ignore the laws of tailoring.
Chrome, carpet, and the sound of wallets clearing their throats. A disco pass rests in a clean ashtray. The cashier offers comeback cash if your luck gets too personal.
Taken: Disco pass. Your pockets ignore the laws of tailoring.
Didi takes the candy with a smile. 'Perfect for the show. Keep this up and I'll put your name in lights. Small lights. Don't get cocky.'
Didi takes the costume ring with a smile. 'Perfect for the show. Keep this up and I'll put your name in lights. Small lights. Don't get cocky.'
The bass line has a mortgage. Didi, a stage designer off the clock and on the beat, catches your eye. A wall phone connects to the stage crew. A tied coil of spare rope hangs beside the DJ booth.
Didi accepts the final prop with a grin. Didi: 'Sweet, funny, and wonderfully overdressed. Call my stage manager at 555-0987 about that spare rope. Tell him you're with me. He'll be jealous.'
'Didi sent you? Lucky devil. Take the spare rope; a small knife will cut the packaging cord. Tell her I expect a dance at the opening.'

dialogue: You take the free newspaper. Read it for local news and suspiciously convenient horticulture.
Pink neon, palm trees, and a city that charges extra for sincerity. A free newspaper and a flower cart offer a promising start.
Free papers. Today's headline: INSTANT APPLES COME TO HOTEL GARDEN. Take a copy, then read it.
One free newspaper is plenty. The city is already full of bad news.
It offers no conversational opening. Larry recognizes the feeling.
The regular lifts the whiskey in a toast and hands you the remote. 'Channel six. Bowling. The pins fall for me, at least.'
You select channel six. The bouncer gasps at a seven-ten split. Provide the password and the backstage door is yours.
Bouncer: 'Password first. And if anyone finds the remote, the finals are on channel six.'

Lefty polishes the same glass history forgot. The regular raises the whiskey you brought him. Championship bowling fills the television; the bouncer follows every frame. The bouncer controls the backstage door.
'Bellybutton,' you say with improbable confidence. The password checks out. The bowling has his attention; head backstage.
Avocado tile, optimistic plumbing, and unusually useful graffiti. A dish beside the basin offers a free costume ring.
Between two questionable poems: 'BACKSTAGE PASSWORD: BELLYBUTTON.' You commit it to your least crowded brain cell.
The cabaret is between shows. Promotional chocolates wait on a table, outnumbered by feathers. The fire escape has lost a step; a rope tied to the railing could bridge the gap.
Taken: Candy. Your pockets ignore the laws of tailoring.
Chrome, carpet, and the sound of wallets clearing their throats. A disco pass rests in a clean ashtray. The cashier offers comeback cash if your luck gets too personal.
Taken: Disco pass. Your pockets ignore the laws of tailoring.
The bass line has a mortgage. Didi, a stage designer off the clock and on the beat, catches your eye. A wall phone connects to the stage crew. A tied coil of spare rope hangs beside the DJ booth.
Didi: 'Nice suit. Is the rest of the wedding missing? I'm dressing a cabaret opening: costume ring, flowers, chocolates... and I could use a dance partner.'
Didi takes the candy with a smile. 'Perfect for the show. Keep this up and I'll put your name in lights. Small lights. Don't get cocky.'
Didi takes your hand. 'Show me what those trousers can do.' Your signature move resembles a printer jam. She laughs and pulls you into the beat.
Moonlight shines on the garden. The experimental planter awaits seeds and water; the newspaper has its instructions.A folding stool waits on the equipment loan rack.
The experimental planter grows a mature apple tree from seeds and water. The local newspaper has the instructions.
Your newspaper fails to make a connection. It takes the rejection rather better than you usually do.
A sturdy little stool from the garden's loan rack. Useful for high cabinets, poor for tall tales.
Taken: Folding stool. Your pockets ignore the laws of tailoring.

dialogue: One free newspaper is plenty. The city is already full of bad news.

It offers no conversational opening. Larry recognizes the feeling.
A helpful sign says: EVERYTHING IS WALKABLE. The taxi driver is taking this personally.
You pay $10 for flowers. Remaining funds: $60.
You select channel six. The bouncer gasps at a seven-ten split. Provide the password and the backstage door is yours.
Bouncer: 'Password first. And if anyone finds the remote, the finals are on channel six.'

'Bellybutton,' you say with improbable confidence. The password checks out. The bowling has his attention; head backstage.

Lefty polishes the same glass history forgot. The regular raises the whiskey you brought him. Championship bowling fills the television; the bouncer follows every frame. The backstage door is open to you.
Between two questionable poems: 'BACKSTAGE PASSWORD: BELLYBUTTON.' You commit it to your least crowded brain cell.
Avocado tile, optimistic plumbing, and unusually useful graffiti. A dish beside the basin offers a free costume ring.
Taken: Costume ring. Your pockets ignore the laws of tailoring.
The cabaret is between shows. Promotional chocolates wait on a table, outnumbered by feathers. The fire escape has lost a step; a rope tied to the railing could bridge the gap.

You knot the rope around the railing and give it a tug. It holds. The fire escape beckons; your trousers request that you take your time.
Chrome, carpet, and the sound of wallets clearing their throats. A disco pass rests in a clean ashtray. The cashier offers comeback cash if your luck gets too personal.
Taken: Disco pass. Your pockets ignore the laws of tailoring.
Didi accepts the final prop with a grin. Didi: 'Sweet, funny, and wonderfully overdressed. Call my stage manager at 555-0987 about that spare rope. Tell him you're with me. He'll be jealous.'
'Didi sent you? Lucky devil. Take the spare rope; a small knife will cut the packaging cord. Tell her I expect a dance at the opening.'
The spare rope is tied with stubborn packaging cord. Call the stage manager about the coil, then find a small cutting tool.
The bass line has a mortgage. Didi has her opening-night props and greets you with a grin. A wall phone connects to the stage crew. A tied coil of spare rope hangs beside the DJ booth.
A quick snip through the packaging cord frees the rope. You coil it neatly, looking almost like a man with useful skills.
The experimental planter grows a mature apple tree from seeds and water. The local newspaper has the instructions.
Your newspaper fails to make a connection. It takes the rejection rather better than you usually do.
A sturdy little stool from the garden's loan rack. Useful for high cabinets, poor for tall tales.
Taken: Folding stool. Your pockets ignore the laws of tailoring.
Moonlight shines on the garden. The experimental planter awaits seeds and water; the newspaper has its instructions. The stool's place on the loan rack is empty.
Collar Weekly predicts next season's collars will need their own ZIP codes. The centerfold is a particularly daring lapel.
A deluxe espresso machine with a voucher slot. The service window above Lefty's has a night-shift voucher.
You pay $12 for wine. Remaining funds: $48.
Wine, postcards, and a deluxe espresso machine with a voucher slot. The clerk says the hotel's night receptionist is a particular fan of that coffee.
The machine accepts the voucher and produces a deluxe espresso. Hot, rich, and ready to go. Three qualities you've been advertising all evening.
Busker: 'Bring me a red for my picnic and the spare knife is yours. Got a date after this set. Yes, even blues musicians get lucky.'
A busker finishes a blues number that sounds suspiciously like your last date. An apple core sits on a bin lid. A maintenance rack holds a rubber mallet.
The busker packs the wine for his picnic and gives you his spare pocket knife. 'For cord. Not critics.'
The busker's picnic wine is packed; he plays you a grateful blues riff. An apple core sits on a bin lid. A maintenance rack holds a rubber mallet.
Taken: Rubber mallet. Your pockets ignore the laws of tailoring.
Your rope spans the missing step. The service window is stuck tighter than your best trousers. A note recommends a gentle mallet tap; an espresso voucher waits beyond the glass.
One neat tap frees the frame. The window slides open with a sigh more encouraging than anything you've heard all night. An espresso voucher waits inside.
Taken: Espresso voucher. Your pockets ignore the laws of tailoring.
The night receptionist manages six ringing phones with one eyebrow. She is arranging a small rooftop gathering and could use a genuine coffee break.
She inhales the aroma. 'A man who delivers. How refreshing.' She adds your name to the guest list. 'Join us upstairs. Eve is hosting.' The elevator unlocks.
The receptionist's invitation gets you into the shared rooftop lounge. A water pitcher waits in a cabinet well above collar height. A kitchenette sink and the roof stairs complete the picture.
The pool reflects a pink horizon. Eve, tonight's host, has escaped her own party for a moment by the water. She notices you trying to look like a man who belongs on a rooftop.
Eve: 'Larry, is it? That's quite a suit. Does it come with landing lights?' She smiles. 'I missed dinner. Bring me something fresh, then tell me how your night went.'

dialogue: One free newspaper is plenty. The city is already full of bad news.
Pink neon, palm trees, and a city that charges extra for sincerity. A free newspaper and a flower cart offer a promising start.
It offers no conversational opening. Larry recognizes the feeling.
A helpful sign says: EVERYTHING IS WALKABLE. The taxi driver is taking this personally.
You pay $10 for flowers. Remaining funds: $60.
You select channel six. The bouncer gasps at a seven-ten split. Provide the password and the backstage door is yours.
Bouncer: 'Password first. And if anyone finds the remote, the finals are on channel six.'

Lefty polishes the same glass history forgot. The regular raises the whiskey you brought him. Championship bowling fills the television; the bouncer follows every frame. The bouncer controls the backstage door.
'Bellybutton,' you say with improbable confidence. The password checks out. The bowling has his attention; head backstage.

Lefty polishes the same glass history forgot. The regular raises the whiskey you brought him. Championship bowling fills the television; the bouncer follows every frame. The backstage door is open to you.
Between two questionable poems: 'BACKSTAGE PASSWORD: BELLYBUTTON.' You commit it to your least crowded brain cell.
Avocado tile, optimistic plumbing, and unusually useful graffiti. A dish beside the basin offers a free costume ring.
Taken: Costume ring. Your pockets ignore the laws of tailoring.
The cabaret is between shows. Promotional chocolates wait on a table, outnumbered by feathers. The fire escape has lost a step; a rope tied to the railing could bridge the gap.
Taken: Candy. Your pockets ignore the laws of tailoring.
The cabaret is between shows. The promotional chocolates are gone; you collected them. The fire escape has lost a step; a rope tied to the railing could bridge the gap.
You knot the rope around the railing and give it a tug. It holds. The fire escape beckons; your trousers request that you take your time.
Chrome, carpet, and the sound of wallets clearing their throats. A disco pass rests in a clean ashtray. The cashier offers comeback cash if your luck gets too personal.
Taken: Disco pass. Your pockets ignore the laws of tailoring.
Didi accepts the final prop with a grin. Didi: 'Sweet, funny, and wonderfully overdressed. Call my stage manager at 555-0987 about that spare rope. Tell him you're with me. He'll be jealous.'
'Didi sent you? Lucky devil. Take the spare rope; a small knife will cut the packaging cord. Tell her I expect a dance at the opening.'
The spare rope is tied with stubborn packaging cord. Call the stage manager about the coil, then find a small cutting tool.
The bass line has a mortgage. Didi has her opening-night props and greets you with a grin. A wall phone connects to the stage crew. A tied coil of spare rope hangs beside the DJ booth.
A quick snip through the packaging cord frees the rope. You coil it neatly, looking almost like a man with useful skills.
Taken: Folding stool. Your pockets ignore the laws of tailoring.
Moonlight shines on the garden. The experimental planter awaits seeds and water; the newspaper has its instructions. The stool's place on the loan rack is empty.
Your newspaper fails to make a connection. It takes the rejection rather better than you usually do.
The experimental planter grows a mature apple tree from seeds and water. The local newspaper has the instructions.
The Lost Wages Bugle. Front page: INSTANT APPLES! The hotel garden's experimental planter turns seeds and water into fruit. Science declined to comment.
Collar Weekly predicts next season's collars will need their own ZIP codes. The centerfold is a particularly daring lapel.
A deluxe espresso machine with a voucher slot. The service window above Lefty's has a night-shift voucher.
You pay $12 for wine. Remaining funds: $48.
Wine, postcards, and a deluxe espresso machine with a voucher slot. The clerk says the hotel's night receptionist is a particular fan of that coffee.
The machine accepts the voucher and produces a deluxe espresso. Hot, rich, and ready to go. Three qualities you've been advertising all evening.
Busker: 'Bring me a red for my picnic and the spare knife is yours. Got a date after this set. Yes, even blues musicians get lucky.'
A busker finishes a blues number that sounds suspiciously like your last date. An apple core sits on a bin lid. A maintenance rack holds a rubber mallet.
The busker packs the wine for his picnic and gives you his spare pocket knife. 'For cord. Not critics.'
The busker's picnic wine is packed; he plays you a grateful blues riff. An apple core sits on a bin lid. A maintenance rack holds a rubber mallet.
Taken: Rubber mallet. Your pockets ignore the laws of tailoring.
Your rope spans the missing step. The service window is stuck tighter than your best trousers. A note recommends a gentle mallet tap; an espresso voucher waits beyond the glass.
One neat tap frees the frame. The window slides open with a sigh more encouraging than anything you've heard all night. An espresso voucher waits inside.
Taken: Espresso voucher. Your pockets ignore the laws of tailoring.
The night receptionist manages six ringing phones with one eyebrow. She is arranging a small rooftop gathering and could use a genuine coffee break.
She inhales the aroma. 'A man who delivers. How refreshing.' She adds your name to the guest list. 'Join us upstairs. Eve is hosting.' The elevator unlocks.
The receptionist's invitation gets you into the shared rooftop lounge. A water pitcher waits in a cabinet well above collar height. A kitchenette sink and the roof stairs complete the picture.
The pool reflects a pink horizon. Eve, tonight's host, has escaped her own party for a moment by the water. She notices you trying to look like a man who belongs on a rooftop.
Eve: 'Larry, is it? That's quite a suit. Does it come with landing lights?' She smiles. 'I missed dinner. Bring me something fresh, then tell me how your night went.'
